text: This jet just dropped twenty-six thousand feet in about one minute.
It was a Learjet 60, flying from Austin, Texas to the Bahamas with nine people on board.
High over Florida, at thirty-five thousand feet, it flew through a strong storm.
The crew reported a light coat of ice and moderate turbulence. Outside, it was minus forty-seven degrees Celsius.
They asked to climb higher. Moments later, they called mayday.
The jet was going too fast and dropping twenty thousand feet a minute.
It came down on a busy road in Greenacres, Florida. All nine people on board died.
No one on the ground was reported hurt. So what can make a jet fall like that? Here are four things investigators will look at.
One: the storm. A strong gust inside a storm can shove a jet's nose down, or roll it on its side, in seconds.
Nose down, a sleek jet like this speeds up fast, past the top speed it was built for.
Two: ice. Tiny ice crystals can plug the tube that measures speed, so the gauge shows the wrong number.
If the pilots trust that number, they can push the jet the wrong way without knowing it.
Three: the speed itself. Near the speed of sound, a shock wave forms on the wing and can pull the nose down even harder.
Four: breaking apart. At that speed, the air can tear parts off the tail or wings, and then there's no pulling out.
The NTSB will dig through the radio calls, the radar, the weather, and every piece of the wreck.
Their report will tell us which one it was. Subscribe so you don't miss what they find.
